A message to parents from 
The most precious gift in the world is a new baby. To your little one, you are 
the center of the universe. And by following your most basic instincts to touch, 
hold, and talk to your baby, you provide the best start to a happy, healthy life. 
Our baby products encourage parents to care for and nurture their children 
through the importance of touch, developing a deep, loving bond that 
transcends all others. 
Parenting is not an exact science, nor is it a one-size-fits-all formula. For more 
than a hundred years, Johnson & Johnson has supported the healthcare needs 
of parents and healthcare professionals, and we understand that all parents feel 
more confident in their role when they have information they can trust. 
That is why we offer this book as our commitment to you to provide 
scientifically sound, professionally reviewed guidance on the important topics 
of pregnancy, baby care, and child development. 
As you read through this book, the most important thing to remember is this: 
you know your baby better than anyone else. By watching, listening, and 
having confidence in your natural ability, you will know how to use the 
information you have in your hands, for the benefit of the baby in your arms.

There is nothing quite like the moment when you find out you're going to be a

Prenatal classes 
As well as prenatal appointments, 
you can go with your partner to 
prenatal classes. At these classes, you 
will learn about all aspects of labor 
and birth and have the opportunity 
to discuss your most intimate 
concerns. Few men are comfortable 
with terms such as "placenta," 
"membranes," "engagement," and 
"cervix." It's one thing to know the 
facts of life from high-school biology 
class and quite another to 
understand in detail how your 
partner's body will actually give birth 
to your baby. At these classes you 
will also begin to learn about how 
you can help during labor. There 
may be practical demonstrations, 
such as ways you can hold your 
partner to help her relax and breathe 
during contractions. 
Another advantage to attending 
these classes is that you will meet 
other expectant fathers whose concerns 
about all the changes in their lives 
may be much the same as yours. 
There is strength in numbers. Some 
of the most enduring friendships 
have started at prenatal classes.

By attending prenatal classes, you will 
get yourself much better equipped to help 
your partner through labor and birth.

Don't be afraid to face them and 
talk them through with your partner. 
This isn't the time for secrets, and 
you will probably find that she has 
been worrying about the same

the baby are not unusual. They

How can I support my partner 
during pregnancy? 
When your partner is pregnant, you are her main support. The child growing inside 
her is a responsibility you have taken on together. You are still partners and lovers 
and best friends, but now there is something new. You are soon to be parents, too, 
and it's important that you are as supportive of each other as you can be. 
Your partner's worries 
Part of the support you offer is about being prepared 
for your partner to have ups and downs. Her body 
is undergoing a huge hormonal upheaval, and this 
often results in mood swings and reactions to trivial 
things that in any other circumstances might seem 
unreasonable. Be patient and understanding. It's 
good practice for parenthood. 
You may find that she is worrying that the shape 
and size of her body make her unattractive. She 
may feel vulnerable and need your reassurance in 
words and deeds. Show your partner that she is 
still your lover as well as the bearer of your baby. 
Time together 
Make time, amid the preparations for the new 
member of the family, to enjoy each other's company 
with nights out, long lunches and, if possible, a 
vacation. If this is a first baby, it may be some time 
before you will have the chance to be on your 
own together again without the complications 
of babysitters and bottles of expressed milk. 
Such concerns are all part of growing 
into the role of father that you 
have taken on.

demonstrate your feelings for your

Is it safe to make love when my 
partner is pregnant? 
There is no reason to curtail your sex life 
during a healthy pregnancy, but if your 
partner is thought to be at high risk of 
miscarriage, or if she has a previous 
history of miscarriages, seek advice from 
your healthcare provider. You may have 
to abstain during the early months while 
the pregnancy establishes itself. 
Are there positions that are better 
during pregnancy? 
This varies from individual to individual. 
It's all about exploring what is best, 
most loving, and most enjoyable for you 
and your partner. Don't be afraid to be 
experimental, especially since, in later 
pregnancy, the missionary position may 
be uncomfortable or impractical. 
Might penetrative sex harm the baby? 
Penetrative sex does not pose any risk to 
the baby. It is safe in the cushion of its 
amniotic sack, which cannot be pierced by 
your penis or entered by your sperm. 
Sometimes men get confused between 
their desire to make love to their partner 
and their fear of harming their child in the 
womb. It is important to disentangle these 
because, particularly in the middle trimester 
of pregnancy, many women experience 
heightened sex drive due to the high level 
of circulating hormones. 
Do all women want to make love 
during pregnancy? 
No. It varies from woman to woman. 
So it is possible your partner may say 
"no" for nine months. She may, however, 
appreciate a massage or a supportive 
hug instead, as a way of maintaining a 
loving physical bond with you. 
Might sex in the later stages of 
pregnancy trigger labor? 
Not on its own. If the baby is ready to 
come, though, sex may be one factor in

hurrying it along. Orgasm does exercise 
the uterine muscles and might cause 
contractions later on in pregnancy, but 
these will die down after a few minutes.

Start off on the right foot and put 
your partner and your baby first. 
Take being a provider seriously—it's 
one of nature's oldest roles for men. 
But so is being a father, so don't be

The birth 
The birth of your child is a major event in your life. It is the end of the 
waiting after nine months and the start of a new life, the formal beginning 
of a relationship, the first page of a lifelong story. Many men now 
choose to be present at the births of their children. 
Your role 
But what is your role during birth, 
and who are you there for—yourself, 
your partner, or your newborn child? 
The answer should be "all three." You 
are witnessing part of your own 
history. You are supporting the person 
closest to you as she goes through 
what can be a difficult physical and 
emotional experience to give birth to 
the child you have both created and 
nurtured. And you are welcoming a 
new member of your family. 
For many men it is a deeply moving, 
almost miraculous event, but it can 
also be distressing if you see your 
partner in pain, or if you don't 
understand what is happening if

medical complications set in. 
Playing your part 
In order to play a full role, make 
sure you understand the mechanics 
of birth. You will be of little use to 
your partner if you have to keep 
asking her or the doctor or midwife 
what is happening. 
You should also take time to talk 
through with your partner how she 
wants to handle the birth and pain 
relief. She may have written down a 
birth plan (see below). When she's 
in the middle of the emotions of 
labor, she will rely on you to make 
her wishes plain to her healthcare 
providers. And, in advance of 
the event, consider realistically how 
you are going to handle your own 
emotions and fears about witnessing 
the birth of your child.

Three stages 
of labor 
The first stage: the cervix opens 
up (dilates) to allow the baby's 
head to pass through. Contractions 
thin, soften, and stretch the cervix. 
Dilation is measured in centimeters, 
up to a maximum of around 10. 
This can be a long process, 
especially with a first labor. 
The second stage: this is shorter, 
usually no more than two hours. 
Your partner will feel a reflex to 
push down during contractions. 
Gradually the baby's head will 
appear, leading to delivery. 
The third stage: this lasts from 
delivery until the uterus contracts 
again to expel the placenta— 
usually after 15 minutes or so.

dads have taken successfully. 
• Work part-time and 
decreasing the family's spending 
Children value your time and 
attention more than a big house, 
a big car, and expensive vacations. 
• Go freelance You can set up an 
office at home and organize your 
own timetable so you are around 
more often during the day. 
• Get out of the fast lane Tell 
your boss that you'll be glad to 
work regular hours but don't want 
to put in overtime in order to be 
promoted. 
• Consider a job-share Working 
moms do it, so why not dads? 
There will be financial implications, 
but also benefits. 
• Stay at home In increasing 
numbers, couples are deciding 
that the dad will stay at home 
and the mom will go out to work. 
58 Being a dad 
Checklist 
Follow these guidelines when it 
comes to disciplining your toddler. 
• Do make your demands simply 
and dearly. 
• Do say "because I say so" when 
you've run out of alternatives. 
• Do give more praise than criticism. 
Be specific with your praise: "Thank 
you for picking up your toys." 
• Do reserve any scolding for when 
you are out of earshot of others. 
• Don't use put-downs. 
• Don't compare your child with 
another "better" one. 
• Don't try to guilt-trip him about 
how hard life is for you. 
• Don't humiliate him by criticizing 
him in front of other children.

able to follow a simple cake recipe

better than a three-year-old and 
so win his admiration. If the cake is 
a flop, turn it into a mutual joke. 
And if all else fails, get a box of cake 
mix from the supermarket so that 
half the hard work is already done 
before you start. 
It doesn't matter what it is you're 
doing as long as the opportunity is 
there for closeness just to happen, 
for your conversation to wander 
into deeper realms, for questions 
and concerns to pop out of his 
mouth, for you to be able to 
influence him in a positive way. 
Let it go 
There are two factors to bear in 
mind when choosing your "dad 
activity" with your toddler. 
• Don't expect to complete what 
you've started. It's the doing, not the 
finishing, that counts. If an end result 
is important, wait until he (inevitably) 
wanders off to find mom and you 
can complete it on your own. 
DON'T MISS OUT 
As your baby reaches the milestones 
of toddlerhood, make sure you are 
there to share in his achievements. 
• Make a choice between your 
standards and your child. For 
example, if you’re gardening together, 
accept that you probably won't end 
up with a neat row of seedlings in 
the flower bed after your child helps 
you plant the seeds. If that's what 
you want, you should find another 
activity to do with your toddler. 
Toddlers and preschoolers 59 
A MASCULINE JOB 
Staying at home to bring up children 
is becoming an increasingly acceptable 
and respected male role. 
Stay-at-home dads 
Although numbers remain tiny, more 
and more men are deciding to put 
being a parent ahead of their careers 
and opting to stay at home and care 
for their children. Some men have 
partners who earn more than they 
do, so it makes more sense for them 
to do this. Others do it because they 
want to. They report that it is deeply 
satisfying, although there may be 
some social isolation to overcome. 
Moms may be getting used to 
stay-at-home dads, but our ongoing 
preoccupation with gender makes 
them nervous about inviting "house- 
husbands" over for coffee while the 
children play. And male friends may 
tease you for being unmasculine, but 
it's hard to think of anything more 
masculine than being a good father. 
Single dads 
Single dads usually fall into two 
main categories: the bereaved 
and the divorced. Whatever 
the reasons, the number of 
households in which children 
live mainly with their father is 
increasing, and reveals a growing 
social and legal awareness that a 
single father can be just as able, 
loving, and effective in bringing 
up children as a single mother. 
Being a single dad isn't easy, but 
developing a support network 
of friends, relatives, community 
organizations, and healthcare 
professionals can give you 
practical and emotional support. 
Your child's pediatrician is a good 
place to start; he or she may be 
able to put you in touch with 
other single dads in your area. 
Questions & Answers 
As a child, my dad was the one who 
handed out the discipline. I don't 
want to fall into that role, but 
when my toddler is running riot, I 
can feel myself heading in that 
direction. How do I avoid this? 
Your own upbringing inevitably has an 
impact on your ideas of parenting, but 
don't automatically use your own father 
as a model for your parenting style. 
Discipline is important, but you must find 
ways that work for you and for your child. 
Talk to your partner and come up with a 
strategy that you both apply equally. 
Should I be disciplining my toddler, 
or is it too early to worry about it? 
No, it's not too early. Your child needs to 
start developing inner controls and learning 
how to negotiate and get along with 
others. Positive example is the biggest part 
of this, but discipline can back it up. 
What do I do when my toddler just 
will not do what I ask him to? 
Try to stay calm, even if others are watching. 
Take your child gently to a quiet spot away 
from the scene of the conflict. If he won t 
move, kneel down next to him and use a

soft, reasonable voice. Explain why you are 
asking him to do something, and ask 
him to think about what he is doing and 
why he is doing it. With many children, 
this diffuses a potential conflict. 
I have lost my temper and shouted 
at my toddler. Now I feel guilty. 
Is this healthy? 
All of us crack at some stage. No parent 
is perfect, however they may appear. Don't 
be too tough on yourself. If you feel 
yourself boiling over, take time out. Go to 
another part of the room where you can 
keep an eye on your child and wait until 
your frustration has subsided. 
60 Being a dad 
How can I avoid being a weekend dad? 
As the role of fathers has changed and their desire has grown to be ever more involved as 
equal co-parents with their partners in the upbringing of their children, society, lawmakers, 
and employers have struggled to keep up. Today, millions of fathers are being turned into 
weekend dads because of a culture of long working hours in our society. So how do you 
avoid becoming a weekend dad? 
Know your rights 
Family leave policies that include a father's right 
to take time off from work in order to spend time 
with a newborn and support his partner vary 
from place to place. Some policies are more 
generous than others. Find out what the law is in 
your area and then speak with your employer 
about taking time off. 
Stand your ground 
Rights are one thing, demanding them another. Male 
colleagues may tease you or resent the time off you 
get when they are still working hard at their desks 
or workstations. Managers may question your 
commitment to your career. If you really want to be 
there for your children, you need to be a committed 
advocate. Explain that you can have two loyalties— 
to work and to family—and that it is all about 
balance. Be prepared for adverse comments. 
WORKING AT HOME 
If you work at home at least some of the time, you will 
inevitably be around your children much more than if you 
work in an office five days a week. 
Avoid guilt 
At times, you may feel you're being torn in two— 
between home and work, your partner and your 
career, being a dad and making financial provisions 
for your family. Some feelings of guilt may enter 
into the equation. Try to resist it at all costs so that 
it does not diminish either side of your life. Push 
for the best work/life balance you can achieve, but 
don't beat yourself up if it's not perfect. 
GETTING INVOLVED 
Taking a career break to stay home and care for your child 
will give you a chance to be more involved in her life. 
Consider the alternatives 
If your employers really are making it tough 
for you to be the kind of dad you want to be, 
consider the alternatives (see page 57). A growing 
number of men take a career break and stay at 
home while their partners go out to work. They 
report that it is deeply satisfying. Other alternatives 
include stepping off the promotional ladder, 
working part-time, or working freelance so you 
can choose your own hours.
